title: Define the Relationship
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Andrew Marcinek pushes back on the idea that banning phones and pulling Chromebooks is a sufficient plan for kids and technology. Using his own history with food and fad diets as an analogy, he argues that elimination is a countdown to quitting, and that young people kept away from technology are unprepared for a digital working life. He endorses screen-free weekends and phone-free family time but calls them practices inside a relationship rather than a replacement for one. He points to pediatric research that has shifted from counting minutes to asking about context, and to the largest study of school phone bans, which found students felt better but attention and learning barely moved. He then announces Think Forward's Define the Relationship toolkit, with guidance for teachers, school leaders, parents and students, built on the five pillars of the Recalibration Framework.
points: Bans are simple and make headlines, but like fad diets they are unsustainable and teach no skill for living with the thing that was removed.
Context questions such as where the screen is, who is in the room, whether the child is making or being fed something, and what happens at bedtime matter more than minutes.
The largest study of school phone bans found improved student mood but almost no gain in attention or learning, so removal is not the same as understanding.
Marcinek's own upbringing of limited exposure with adult attention, such as a clock on the Nintendo and Oregon Trail at school, is offered as a model that was neither ban nor free-for-all.
The new toolkit targets four audiences at once and moves schools from blanket rules to a default-off posture with purposeful exceptions.
quotes: Neither of us got healthier by swearing off food, because that is not a plan a person can live inside. What we had to do was something slower and more annoying: figure out what we were eating, when, why, and in whose company, and then rebuild the relationship one decision at a time until the good decisions stopped feeling like decisions.
But walking away is a practice that lives inside a relationship. It is not a substitute for one.

It may work for the families fortunate enough to pull it off, but a plan that only works for the fortunate is not a plan for a school, and it is far from a silver bullet for the challenges we face every day in classrooms and at kitchen tables.
Eliminating every single thing that brings you occasional joy is not a long-term plan. It is a countdown to the day you quit the plan.

None of that was a ban, and none of it was a free-for-all. It was exposure with an adult paying attention, and it is the reason I ended up in this field and the reason I am leaning so hard into this subject now.

The largest study of school phone bans to date, published this spring, found the same thing from the other direction: locking phones away made students feel better, which is real and worth having, but it did almost nothing for attention or learning. Removing the thing is not the same as understanding it.

We are not aiming for perfection here; we are aiming for an intentional connection that has to be taught. If we want real progress in our schools and in our homes, our job is not to banish the tech. It is to recalibrate our relationship with it.
